claims.text: Adding a moderate concentration of a transition metal to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy will improve its glass-forming ability.
Adding a moderate concentration of a transition metal will improve the thermal stability of the alloy's amorphous state.
Ni or Fe has a high mixing enthalpy with phosphorus.
Rapid-cooling processes such as melt spinning or splat quenching are typical processing routes for glass formation.
The beneficial effect is expected only when the added transition metal does not exceed its solubility limit.
The beneficial effect is expected only when the added transition metal does not induce crystallization during cooling.
Adding the transition metal enhances atomic-level chemical disorder.
Adding the transition metal makes the mixing enthalpy between phosphorus and the transition metal more negative.
Enhanced chemical disorder and negative phosphorus–transition-metal mixing enthalpy suppress nucleation and growth of crystalline phases.
Transition-metal–phosphorus interactions increase chemical complexity and local structural frustration.
Increased chemical complexity and local structural frustration raise the energy barrier for crystallization.
A raised crystallization barrier thermally stabilizes the amorphous phase.
The modified alloy will have a higher critical cooling rate for glass formation than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the baseline alloy.
Excessive transition-metal concentration or formation of stable phosphorus-containing intermetallic compounds may eliminate the improvements in glass-forming ability and thermal stability.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis seeks improved glass-forming ability, but the predicted outcome and falsification rule treat a higher critical cooling rate as improvement. Improved glass-forming ability is ordinarily represented by a lower required critical cooling rate, so the direction of this outcome is internally inconsistent with the stated goal and nucleation-suppression mechanism.
